newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-Disclosure rules won't hurt Enerco-CEO.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Disclosure rules won't hurt Enerco-CEO.

text.p: New Zealand gas distributor and retailer Enerco is more likely to benefit than suffer from new disclosure regulations aimed at increasing competition in the industry, chief executive Kevin Johnson said on Tuesday.
The new information disclosure regulations will come into force on August 7 and focus on the natural monopolies in pipeline businesses.
"There's no surprises in the this. We knew it was coming," Johnson told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"Certainly as far as Enerco is concerned, we've been working in an environment, probably for the last six months to a year, where we've pretty much assumed that disclosure is in place."
Under the new regulations, gas companies will be required to disclose separate financial statements for transmission, wholesale, distribution and retail businesses.
Energy Minister Max Bradford said earlier in the day he expected the regulations to foster more competition between gas retailers and produce benefits for consumers.
"Perhaps more important, however, is the prospect of new wholesalers entering the market," he said.
Johnson said competition was already taking place.
"People have been free to come into the market and compete against us, and indeed, that's what been happening in the Auckland market already," he said.
"We have somebody else (Power New Zealand )who's is supplying gas to what used to be our customers through our network, which is exactly in line with what Bradford's talking about here."
The new regulations were in effect a veiled threat from the government, reminding the industry that if it did not behave competitively, legislation would be introduced to ensure it did.
Johnson said he did not expect Enerco's bottom-line profit to suffer as a result of the government's move.
"We don't see that at all. If anything, we would see it being enhanced because it provides us with the opportunity to move outside of our traditional supply areas and compete in the other areas.

"We've been confined to Wellington, Auckland, Palmerston North and Hawkes Bay. Under the new regulations, or the deregulated market, we can go anywhere. So if anything, it is going to enhance our bottom line," he said.
But Johnson said Enerco was starting to feel the effects of the sluggish New Zealand economy.

"We are finding the impact of the current economic situation is starting to come through, particularly with our business customers," he said. "It's not a dramatic change, but certainly it's quite different to what it was 12 months ago."
He said medium-sized companies in particular were using less gas than previously.
"Where they were running three shifts they might be back to two. Where they might have been flat out 12 months ago, they're now perhaps at 80 percent of what they were.

"Those companies involved in export are coming under pressure and they might be looking at a different product mix for example. Sometimes that has a positive effect, sometimes it has a negative effect. But there's no question, things are definitely slower than what they were 12 months ago," he said.
However, Enerco was not reviewing its profit projections at this stage, Johnson said, and was still confident of bettering its 1996/97 year profit of NZ$18.9 million this financial year.
"We think that towards the end of the current financial year things will be starting to pick up again," he said.
